title: Berlin Alexanderplatz
author: Alfred Döblin
note: Berlin, 1929. New English from the German.

scenes.title: With the 41 into the city
scenes.reentry: He stood before the gate of Tegel Prison and was free.

breaths.text: He stood before the gate of Tegel Prison and was free.
Yellow summer coat hanging on him like a sack, too wide in the shoulders, too short in the sleeves.
The others were still out there behind the wall, raking potatoes in rows, backs bent, guards strolling.
Franz Biberkopf stood alone.
The gate clanged shut behind him with a sound like a bank vault.
Iron.
Final.
He didn’t move.
The coat smelled of mothballs and old sweat.
His own sweat from four years back.
You think that’s it, Franz?
One step and the world is yours again?
Don’t kid yourself.
A tram came grinding along the street, number 41, bright red, sparks spitting from the overhead wire.
People inside reading newspapers, women with shopping nets, a boy with a schoolbag.
Normal people.
Franz’s legs wouldn’t carry him.
The tram stopped, doors hissed open, conductor looked at him once, twice, then rang the bell.
The 41 rolled on without Franz Biberkopf.
He stood there.
The gate was closed.
The potatoes were still being raked.
Everything behind him still moved according to rules.
Everything in front of him moved according to no rules at all.
Another 41 came.
This time he grabbed the handrail like a drowning man and swung himself up the steps.
The car was half full.
He squeezed onto the wooden bench between a fat woman in a flowered dress and a man reading the B.Z. am Mittag.
The pain hit him then, right in the middle of the chest, like someone was pulling a tooth with pliers and no cocaine.
Not a tooth in his mouth.
A tooth somewhere deeper.
The city itself, maybe.
Or what was left of him.
“Alexanderplatz next stop but three,” the conductor called.
Berlin rushed at him.
Houses, chimneys, advertisements, everything screaming.
Kaffee HAG.
Drink it and sleep like a baby.
BOSCH spark plugs.
Wrigley’s Spearmint.
The flavor lasts.
Vote List 4 Social Democrats.
Lanolin cream for soft hands.
The red-white-blue posters of the Reichsbanner.
A horse pulling a beer wagon, hooves ringing on the pavement like pistol shots.
Franz stared out the window.
The tram rattled over the tracks, swayed around curves.
Every jolt went straight into that pulled-tooth place.
He kept his fists jammed between his knees.
The fat woman beside him smelled of onions and cheap perfume.
She glanced at his yellow coat, at his prison haircut, at the way he sat like a man expecting to be hit.
“You all right, mister? ”
He didn’t answer.
Couldn’t.
The words were still locked up back in Tegel with the potatoes.
You’re out now, Franz.
Four years for manslaughter and here you are riding the 41 like any other citizen.
Congratulations.
The city doesn’t give a damn.
Look at it.
It’s already chewing up the next batch of fools.
The tram passed factories, tenements, a schoolyard where kids screamed during recess.
A Salvation Army band on a corner: trombone, drum, a girl in a poke bonnet shaking a collection box.
“Repent, the Kingdom is at hand!
” The trombone slid into a sour note.
Franz almost laughed.
Almost.
The sound died in his throat.
He saw himself from outside.
Big man in a yellow coat that didn’t fit, sitting among the living, eyes wide like a cow at the slaughterhouse gate.
The iron gates had closed.
That part was true.
But the other gates—the ones in front—those were wide open and howling.
The conductor rang again.
“Schönholzer Straße! ”
Too early.
Franz jumped up anyway.
The fat woman had to pull in her knees.
He stumbled down the steps, almost fell when the tram jerked forward again.
The door slammed.
The 41 rattled away into the traffic, sparks flying, taking its normal people with it.
Now he was standing on the pavement.
Berlin hit him full force.
Noise.
Smell of gasoline, horse piss, coal smoke, frying sausages from a stand.
People shoving past.
A cyclist nearly ran him down.
“Watch where you’re going, you idiot! ”
Franz flinched.
The voice sounded like a guard’s.
He crossed the street without looking, horns blared, a truck swerved.
He reached the other side alive.
Somehow.
He walked.
Legs moving but the rest of him still back at the prison gate.
The yellow coat flapped around his calves.
